category_title: Skillful readers who disengage from remedial instruction but excel in disciplinary inquiry tasks
minimal_context: Aziza is sitting in her Read 180 intervention class and is expected to complete a vocabulary memorization and skill-building worksheet in her notebook.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Aziza, it is time for our Read 180 skill-building activity. Please open your notebook and start the vocabulary memorization section.

STUDENT: (Keeps a paperback novel open on her lap) I read everything, just everything . . . most kids, they’ll read just because the teacher tells them to. When I read, if there’s more to read, I’m going to continue.

TUTOR: Please put the novel away for now and fill in the blanks on your worksheet.

STUDENT: No. It helps me get a free period of class to read.

TUTOR: You need to complete these exercises so you don't have holes in your notebook.

STUDENT: (Rests her head on the desk, ignoring the skill-building activity entirely, and continues reading her unsanctioned novel instead of participating.)

options.A: Focus on community building so that students feel comfortable taking risks, diligently protecting them by ensuring no answer is ever treated as stupid.
options.B: Implement a daily point system for her classwork, with a daily goal set at her earning 80% of the possible points each day.
options.C: Organize instruction around disciplinary inquiry rather than skill building and memorization, teaching historical literacy practices like considering context and reading across documents.
options.D: Provide frequent acknowledgment of her achievements alongside ensuring that the reading and worksheet demands are within her capability.
